justice: The path is wide and paved with a smooth continuous surface, so space is reasonably allocated for general walking and low-speed access.
A parked car and a line of parked motorcycles occupy part of the waterside path, reducing equal access to public space for non-motorized users.
The canal edge is protected by a metal guardrail, which supports basic accessibility and safe shared use, but no tactile paving or marked accessible guidance is visible.
The route appears level without visible steps, which improves barrier-free movement for many users, though the usable width is narrowed by vehicles and planting edges.
safety: The canal side has a continuous railing, which reduces fall risk next to the water.
Motor vehicles are present directly on the pedestrian-priority path, creating conflict risk for walkers and cyclists in a space without lane separation.
The pavement is wide and visibility ahead is long and unobstructed, which helps users detect oncoming people, bicycles, or vehicles.
Street lighting fixtures are visible along the waterside edge, supporting some night safety, but the overall path lacks marked crossings or speed-control features.
livability: Trees, shrubs, and the canal provide a calmer residential atmosphere than a typical traffic street.
The waterfront edge and landscaped planting increase amenity value and make the corridor potentially pleasant for everyday strolling.
The opposite bank shows rubble and a less maintained environment, which weakens the overall neighborhood quality and recreational appeal.
There are no visible benches, play elements, or active ground-floor commercial uses, limiting social activity and everyday street life.
sustainability: Street trees and planting strips contribute modest green infrastructure and local ecological value.
The permeable grass-paver strip near the railing suggests some stormwater infiltration capacity compared with fully sealed pavement.
The setting appears oriented to local access and walking along the canal, but there is no visible public transport stop or dedicated cycling facility supporting broader low-carbon mobility.
Private cars and motorcycles occupying the corridor indicate continued dependence on motorized access within the public realm.
aesthetics: The canal, trees, and planted shrubs create a visually pleasant waterfront composition.
The residential buildings on the left have a relatively consistent height and facade rhythm, giving the street edge coherence.
The decorative metal railing and lamp posts add formal design detail to the waterside space.
Construction debris and a rough-looking opposite bank reduce scenic quality despite the otherwise orderly foreground.
comfort: Trees provide partial shade along the route, improving thermal comfort, but large sections of the path remain exposed to sun.
The concrete pavement looks even and smooth, supporting comfortable walking and rolling.
There are no visible benches or resting facilities, so long stays or breaks are less comfortable.
The corridor appears quiet with little heavy traffic, which likely improves psychological and acoustic comfort.
walkability: The path is wide, level, and continuous, which supports straightforward walking movement.
Landscaping and waterfront views make walking more attractive than in a purely utilitarian service lane.
Parked cars and motorcycles intrude into the walking space, reducing clear pedestrian priority and effective width.
No visible crosswalks, wayfinding, or dedicated pedestrian markings are present, so broader route legibility and connectivity are only moderate.
bikeability: The corridor is physically wide enough for cycling, but there is no marked or protected bike lane.
Parked vehicles on the path create obstacles and force cyclists to mix unpredictably with pedestrians and access traffic.
The surface appears smooth enough for everyday riding, which is a positive physical condition.
No visible bicycle parking, lane symbols, or intersection treatments are present to support convenient and legible cycling use.
